title: sync/atomic & Lock-Free Counters
summary: An **atomic** operation is an indivisible read-modify-write the hardware guarantees no other core can interrupt. The `sync/atomic` package exposes them as lock-free building blocks — and since **Go 1.19** they are *sequentially consistent*, so they not only count without a mutex but also establish happens-before ordering between goroutines.

subtopics.title: Typed atomics (Go 1.19+)
subtopics.explanation: Prefer the wrapper types atomic.Int64, atomic.Uint64, atomic.Int32, atomic.Bool, atomic.Pointer[T], and atomic.Value over the bare functions. They make the variable's atomic-ness part of its type (you can't accidentally read it non-atomically with a plain load), and crucially they guarantee correct 8-byte alignment even on 32-bit platforms.
subtopics.example: var n atomic.Int64; n.Add(1); v := n.Load()

subtopics.title: Add / Load / Store / Swap
subtopics.explanation: Add atomically adds a delta and returns the new value. Load reads the current value atomically. Store writes atomically. Swap atomically writes a new value and returns the old one. Each is a single indivisible operation — no other goroutine can observe a half-written state.
subtopics.example: old := n.Swap(0) // atomically reset, capture previous total

subtopics.title: CompareAndSwap (CAS)
subtopics.explanation: CompareAndSwap(old, new) writes new only if the current value still equals old, returning whether it succeeded. It is the primitive behind lock-free algorithms: you read, compute, then conditionally commit, retrying if someone raced you.
subtopics.example: ok := n.CompareAndSwap(5, 6) // true only if n was still 5

subtopics.title: The CAS retry loop
subtopics.explanation: For any update that depends on the old value (atomic max, atomic clamp, a derived counter) a single Add isn't enough. Load the old value, compute the new one, then CAS; if CAS fails another goroutine won the race, so loop and retry with the fresh value.
subtopics.example: for { old := v.Load(); if v.CompareAndSwap(old, f(old)) { break } }

subtopics.title: Happens-before & alignment
subtopics.explanation: Since Go 1.19 atomics are sequentially consistent: an atomic Store happens-before a later atomic Load that observes it, so they can synchronize data, not just count. Two rules: never mix atomic and plain access to the same variable, and on 32-bit platforms bare 64-bit atomics need 8-byte alignment — the typed wrappers handle that for you.
subtopics.example: // publish config then flag: writers Store, readers Load — ordered

subtopics.title: Atomics vs Mutex vs channels
subtopics.explanation: Use an atomic for a single word (counter, flag, pointer swap) — it's lock-free and scales best under contention. Use a Mutex when you must keep two or more fields consistent together (a multi-variable invariant). Use channels to transfer ownership of data and coordinate goroutines. Atomics give per-variable atomicity, not multi-variable invariants.
subtopics.example: var requests atomic.Int64 // one counter -> atomic, not a mutex

foundations.overview: When two goroutines increment the same counter, a plain `n++` is actually three steps — load, add, store — and two goroutines can interleave those steps and lose an update. The classic fix is a mutex, but for a single machine word the hardware can do better: it offers instructions that perform the whole read-modify-write as one indivisible (atomic) step that no other core can split. The `sync/atomic` package exposes those instructions, letting you build correct, lock-free counters and flags that scale better than a mutex under contention.
foundations.formalDefinition: An atomic operation is an indivisible read-modify-write (or read, or write) on a single memory word that appears to execute instantaneously with respect to all other goroutines; sync/atomic provides such operations (Add, Load, Store, Swap, CompareAndSwap) with sequentially-consistent ordering since Go 1.19.
foundations.whyItMatters: Counters, rate limiters, feature flags, reference counts, and hot-swappable config are everywhere in backend services. Doing them with atomics instead of mutexes removes lock park/unpark overhead on the hot path and is a senior-level distinction interviewers probe for.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a single turnstile with a built-in mechanical counter: each person who passes bumps the count by exactly one, and the mechanism physically cannot register two half-presses at once. CompareAndSwap is like a combination lock that only opens if the dial is still on the number you last saw — if someone moved it, you re-read and try again.
foundations.runtimePerspective: Atomic operations compile down to dedicated CPU instructions (LOCK XADD for Add on x86, LDXR/STXR pairs on ARM) rather than a function call into the scheduler. There's no goroutine parking, no run-queue interaction — just a hardware-level memory barrier. The typed wrappers (atomic.Int64 etc.) are zero-cost abstractions: the same instruction, but with a compiler-enforced guarantee that the field is 8-byte aligned and never touched non-atomically.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Request and error counters in middleware, sequence/ID generators, the 'closed' flag of a connection, reference counting in resource pools, and lock-free configuration hot-swapping via atomic.Pointer/atomic.Value.
foundations.businessImpact: On a high-QPS service, replacing a contended mutex on a metrics counter with an atomic removes a serialization point, which raises throughput and lowers tail latency on the same hardware — directly reducing the fleet size needed to serve the load.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Atomics make intent explicit (this is a single shared word) and, with the typed wrappers, make whole classes of bugs — torn 64-bit reads on 32-bit ARM, accidental non-atomic access — unrepresentable. But misusing them for multi-field invariants causes subtle, race-detector-passing corruption.
foundations.performanceImpact: An uncontended atomic Add is a handful of nanoseconds; a mutex lock/unlock is several times that and can trigger a futex syscall under contention. Under heavy multi-core increment, however, all cores fighting over one cache line causes 'false sharing' / cache-line bouncing, so a single global atomic counter can become a bottleneck — sharded counters then win.
commonUseCases: Lock-free request/error counters in HTTP middleware
Lock-free config hot-swap with atomic.Pointer / atomic.Value
CAS retry loops for atomic max / monotonic sequence IDs

commonMisconceptions.myth: Atomics can make any block of code thread-safe.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They give atomicity for a single word only. Two fields that must stay consistent together still need a Mutex — atomics don't compose into multi-variable invariants.

commonMisconceptions.myth: atomic.AddInt64 on a struct field always works.
commonMisconceptions.reality: On 32-bit platforms the bare 64-bit functions require the field to be 8-byte aligned (e.g. the first word of the struct). The typed atomic.Int64 wrapper guarantees alignment for you — which is why it's the modern default.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can read an atomic variable with a normal load 'just to peek'.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Mixing atomic and non-atomic access to the same variable is a data race with undefined behavior; once a variable is atomic, every access must go through atomic methods.

visualExplorer.title: The CAS retry loop
visualExplorer.caption: How an atomic update that depends on the old value commits — or retries when another goroutine wins the race.

config.intro: Atomically computing a new value from the old one with CompareAndSwap:

steps.name: Load the old value
steps.detail: old := v.Load() reads the current value atomically. This is the value we'll base our computation on.

steps.name: Compute the new value
steps.detail: new := f(old) — e.g. max(old, candidate). This runs on a local copy; the shared variable is untouched so far.

steps.name: Try to commit with CAS
steps.detail: v.CompareAndSwap(old, new) writes new ONLY if v still equals old — proving no one changed it while we computed.

steps.name: Succeeded? Done.
steps.detail: If CAS returns true, our update committed atomically with no lock. Break out of the loop.

steps.name: Failed? Retry.
steps.detail: If CAS returns false, another goroutine changed v first. Loop back, Load the fresh value, and recompute — never blocking, just retrying.

visualExplorer.title: Why atomics skip the scheduler
visualExplorer.caption: A mutex under contention parks goroutines via the runtime scheduler (G/P/M); an atomic op is a single CPU instruction with no parking — which is what makes it lock-free.

interactiveExamples.title: Lock-free counter vs the racy n++
interactiveExamples.explanation: 1000 goroutines each increment 1000 times. A plain n++ loses updates (and trips -race); atomic.Int64.Add is indivisible, so the total is always exactly 1,000,000.

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: an atomic max with a CAS retry loop
interactiveExamples.explanation: Add can't express 'set to the larger value' because the result depends on the old value. Fill in the CAS retry loop: Load the old max, compute the new max, then CompareAndSwap, looping until it sticks.

checkpoints.code:
var n atomic.Int64
n.Store(10)
old := n.Swap(3)
fmt.Println(old, n.Load())
checkpoints.explanation: Swap atomically writes the new value (3) and returns the previous one (10). So old is 10 and the variable now holds 3.

checkpoints.prompt: You need to keep `balance` and `lastTxnID` consistent with each other across goroutines. What should you use?
options: Two atomic.Int64 fields, one per value
A single sync.Mutex guarding both fields
checkpoints.explanation: Atomics give per-variable atomicity, not a multi-variable invariant. Updating two separate atomics is two separate atomic steps, so a reader can observe a new balance with the old txn ID. A Mutex makes the pair update atomic together.

checkpoints.prompt: This CAS loop sometimes loses updates. What's wrong?
options: It Loads then Stores without CompareAndSwap, so a concurrent update between the two is overwritten
checkpoints.explanation: Load then Store is two separate atomic ops with a gap between them. If another goroutine increments in that gap, this Store clobbers it. Either use v.Add(1) (single op) or a CompareAndSwap retry loop that only commits if the value is unchanged.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the line so the update commits only if no one changed v since the Load.
checkpoints.codeAfter:
// loop body ends; break on success
}
checkpoints.explanation: CompareAndSwap(old, next) writes next only if v still equals old, returning success. Breaking on success and retrying on failure is the lock-free update pattern. A plain Store would overwrite a concurrent update.

codeLab.title: Build a lock-free hit counter
codeLab.instructions: Implement a Counter type backed by an atomic.Int64. `Inc()` adds one atomically, `Value()` reads the current total. It must be safe for many goroutines to call Inc concurrently with no lost updates and no data race. Do not use a mutex.
hints: Embed an atomic.Int64 field; its zero value is ready to use, no init needed.
Inc should call Add(1) — a single indivisible operation, not Load+Store.
Value should call Load(); run `go test -race` to confirm there's no data race.

debuggingLab.title: The race detector flags a counter that 'uses atomics'
debuggingLab.symptom: The total is occasionally wrong and `go test -race` reports a data race on the same variable, even though Inc uses atomic.AddInt64.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Inc updates n atomically, but Value reads it with a plain, non-atomic load. Mixing atomic and non-atomic access to the same variable is a data race: the reader may observe a torn or stale value, and the behavior is undefined. Once a variable is shared atomically, EVERY access must go through atomic operations.
commonMistakes: Assuming a plain read is fine 'because it's just reading'.
Using the bare atomic functions on a raw int64 field, which also risks 8-byte alignment problems on 32-bit platforms.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Make every access atomic (and prefer the typed wrapper so misuse is impossible).

theory.question: What does sync/atomic give you, and when would you choose it over a sync.Mutex?
theory.directAnswer: It gives indivisible read-modify-write operations (Add, Load, Store, Swap, CompareAndSwap) on a single machine word, implemented with dedicated CPU instructions and no goroutine parking. Choose an atomic when you're protecting a single word — a counter, flag, or pointer — because it's lock-free and scales better under contention. Choose a Mutex when you must keep two or more fields consistent together, since atomics give per-variable atomicity, not multi-variable invariants.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A package exposing hardware atomic operations and (since Go 1.19) typed wrappers like atomic.Int64, atomic.Bool, and atomic.Pointer[T].
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A plain n++ is load-add-store and can interleave across goroutines, losing updates; the hardware can do the whole thing as one uninterruptible step.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The op compiles to an instruction like LOCK XADD (x86) or an LDXR/STXR loop (ARM) that the CPU guarantees is atomic, with a memory barrier so other goroutines see a consistent view.

theory.whyImportant: Picking the right primitive is a senior judgment call that affects correctness and tail latency on hot paths.
theory.realWorldExample: An HTTP middleware bumps a request counter with atomic.Int64.Add on every request — far cheaper than a mutex around requests++ at high QPS.

followUps.question: Why prefer atomic.Int64 over atomic.AddInt64 on a raw int64?
followUps.answer: The wrapper makes the field's atomic-ness part of its type (you can't read it non-atomically by mistake) and guarantees 8-byte alignment even on 32-bit platforms, where the bare 64-bit functions would otherwise panic on a misaligned field.

followUps.question: Are channels ever the better choice?
followUps.answer: Yes — when you're transferring ownership of data or coordinating goroutine lifecycles. Atomics are for shared single-word state, not for handing work between goroutines.

theory.question: Since Go 1.19, what memory-ordering guarantee do atomics provide, and why does it matter beyond counting?
theory.directAnswer: Go's atomics are sequentially consistent: all goroutines observe atomic operations in a single, total order, and an atomic Store happens-before any later atomic Load that reads its value. That means atomics can synchronize — publishing data, not just counting it. If goroutine A writes a config object and then atomically Stores a pointer to it, a goroutine that atomically Loads that pointer is guaranteed to see the fully-written object.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A memory-ordering model defining what one goroutine is guaranteed to observe about another's atomic operations.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Without an ordering guarantee, the compiler and CPU could reorder surrounding writes, so a reader could see a published pointer before the data it points to was written.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Each atomic op carries a full memory barrier; the happens-before edge from Store to a Load-that-observes-it transitively orders the non-atomic writes that preceded the Store.

theory.whyImportant: This is what makes lock-free config hot-swapping with atomic.Pointer/atomic.Value correct, and it's a frequent advanced interview distinction.
theory.realWorldExample: A server keeps *Config in an atomic.Pointer[Config]; a reload goroutine builds a new immutable Config and Stores the pointer, and every request Loads it lock-free, always seeing a complete, consistent config.

followUps.question: What is the ABA problem?
followUps.answer: In a CAS loop, the value can change from A to B and back to A between your Load and CAS; the CAS succeeds because it only checks equality, even though the world changed underneath you. It bites pointer-recycling algorithms; for plain counters that only ever increase it's not an issue. Mitigations include version/tag counters or hazard pointers.

followUps.question: Can you peek at an atomic with a normal read for performance?
followUps.answer: No — mixing atomic and non-atomic access to the same variable is a data race with undefined behavior. Every access must be atomic.

scenario.question: Your service exposes a single global atomic.Int64 request counter incremented on every request. At high QPS on a 64-core box, profiling shows surprising CPU spent on that increment and throughput plateaus. What's happening and how do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: All cores are contending on the one cache line that holds the counter — every Add must take exclusive ownership of that line, so it bounces between cores' caches (false sharing / cache-line contention). The atomic is correct but has become a hardware bottleneck. Fix it by sharding: keep one padded counter per CPU/shard (each on its own cache line), increment the local shard, and sum the shards when you read. This trades a tiny read-side cost for near-linear write scalability.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Cache-coherence contention on a single hot atomic word.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Atomic writes require exclusive ownership of the cache line; many cores writing the same line serialize on the coherence protocol.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Sharded counters spread writes across many lines (padded to 64 bytes to avoid false sharing), so cores rarely fight over the same line; Value() sums shards.

scenario.whyImportant: It shows you understand that lock-free is not contention-free, a real production scaling issue.
scenario.realWorldExample: High-throughput metrics libraries and the runtime's own memory stats use per-P/sharded counters precisely to avoid this single-line hotspot.

followUps.question: How do you avoid false sharing between shards?
followUps.answer: Pad each shard to a full cache line (e.g. a struct with the atomic.Int64 plus _ [56]byte padding, or [8]int64 alignment) so two shards never share the same 64-byte line.

coding.question: Implement a lock-free, monotonically increasing ID generator: `func (g *IDGen) Next() int64` returns 1, 2, 3, ... and is safe for concurrent callers, with no two callers ever getting the same ID.
coding.thoughtProcess: Each call needs a unique number, so I need an atomic increment that also returns the resulting value. atomic.Int64.Add returns the new value after adding, which is exactly a fetch-and-add. Starting from a zero value, Add(1) hands the first caller 1, the next 2, and so on — indivisibly, so no two callers collide. No mutex, no CAS loop needed because a single Add already returns the post-increment value.
coding.lineByLine: last is an atomic.Int64 whose zero value is 0. Add(1) atomically increments it and returns the new value, so the first call returns 1, the next 2, etc. Because Add is a single indivisible operation that returns its result, two concurrent callers can never observe or be handed the same value — no lock and no CAS retry loop is required.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) per call — one atomic instruction.

followUps.question: Why is a CAS loop unnecessary here but required for an atomic max?
followUps.answer: Add's result doesn't depend on a computation over the old value beyond a fixed delta, and Add already returns the post-op value atomically. An atomic max's new value depends on comparing the candidate to the current value, so you must Load, compare, and conditionally CompareAndSwap, retrying on races.

followUps.question: How would you make IDs unique across process restarts?
followUps.answer: Seed last from a persisted high-water mark (or use a time/epoch-based or distributed scheme like Snowflake), since an in-memory atomic resets to 0 on restart.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Reach for atomics on single-word shared state in hot paths: counters, flags, and copy-on-write config behind atomic.Pointer[T] or atomic.Value. Keep config objects immutable so a reader that Loads the pointer can use it without further locking; reloads build a brand-new object and Store the pointer. Anything needing a multi-field invariant belongs behind a Mutex, not a bag of atomics.
productionDeepDive.performance: An uncontended atomic op is a few nanoseconds and avoids the mutex's potential futex syscall under contention. But a single global atomic counter becomes a cache-line hotspot on many-core machines; shard it (one padded counter per CPU/shard) and sum on read. Always pad shards to a cache line to dodge false sharing.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Never mix atomic and non-atomic access to the same variable — it's a data race. Atomics are sequentially consistent (Go 1.19+), so a Store happens-before a Load that observes it, which is what makes lock-free publication of config correct. Use the CAS retry loop for any update derived from the old value, and beware the ABA problem in pointer-recycling structures.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Prefer the typed wrappers (atomic.Int64, atomic.Pointer[T]) so the compiler guarantees 8-byte alignment on 32-bit platforms and prevents accidental plain access. Run the full test suite with -race in CI; the detector catches mixed atomic/non-atomic access that passes ordinary tests.
productionDeepDive.observability: Atomic counters are the natural backing store for cheap, always-on metrics (requests, errors, in-flight). Read them with Load and export periodically; for high-cardinality hot counters expose the summed sharded value so the metric itself doesn't become a bottleneck.
productionDeepDive.security: When using atomics to gate security-relevant state (a 'revoked' or 'shutting-down' flag), ensure the publishing write and the dependent data use the happens-before edge correctly, so readers can't act on a flag before the data it guards is visible. Don't roll your own lock-free structure for sensitive invariants — a Mutex is easier to reason about and audit.

caseStudies.problem: A single global counter for memory/GC stats serialized all cores on one cache line.
caseStudies.solution: Per-P (per-processor) sharded counters summed on read.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Slightly more memory and a read-side sum, for near-linear write scalability.
caseStudies.lessons: Lock-free is not contention-free; shard hot atomic counters and pad to a cache line.

caseStudies.problem: Reloading configuration without a global lock on every request's read.
caseStudies.solution: Immutable Config behind atomic.Pointer[Config]: readers Load lock-free, reloads Store a fresh pointer.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Whole-object copy on reload (cheap, infrequent) versus zero-cost, contention-free reads.
caseStudies.lessons: Sequentially-consistent atomics make copy-on-write hot-swap correct and lock-free.

keyTakeaways: An atomic operation is an indivisible read-modify-write on a single word; sync/atomic exposes Add, Load, Store, Swap, and CompareAndSwap as lock-free primitives.
Prefer the Go 1.19+ typed wrappers (atomic.Int64, atomic.Bool, atomic.Pointer[T]) — they're sequentially consistent, enforce atomic-only access, and guarantee 8-byte alignment on 32-bit platforms.
Use Add for a simple counter; use the CAS retry loop (Load, compute, CompareAndSwap, retry) for any update derived from the old value, and watch for the ABA problem.

Atomics give per-variable atomicity, not multi-variable invariants: use a Mutex for consistent multi-field updates, channels to transfer ownership, and shard hot counters to avoid cache-line contention.
